title: When the Asset Sings
premise: Marguerite Delacroix, a gifted interpreter who has spent a decade making himself professionally invisible inside a doomed peace delegation, is pulled into an off-the-books operation when his voiceprint—harvested from intercepted calls—unlocks a black server in Tallinn containing evidence that the delegation's failure was engineered. The defector who can prove it, Elena Vasquez, may herself be bait dangled to flush out everyone who knows the truth. As Marguerite smuggles her toward a dawn extraction flight through a city closing around them, he must choose between the duty that defined him and the belonging he never allowed himself. The extraction succeeds only because Marguerite gives up his anonymity forever, surrendering his old identity to save hers—and the final chapter finds him nameless but no longer invisible, alive in a life he chose.
about_author: Kestrel Halloran is the pen name of a former conference interpreter turned novelist who spent years working behind glass booths in negotiation rooms across three continents. They write thrillers about the people history forgets—the translators, couriers, and fixers who stand one sentence away from catastrophe.

chapters.title: The Grammar of Silence
chapters.summary: POV Marguerite. In Geneva, Marguerite interprets a fractious session of the failing peace delegation, smoothing over insults and rendering threats diplomatic. He notices a delegate's coded phrasing and files it away out of habit. Emotional beat: the loneliness of a man whose job is to be no one, establishing his invisibility as both armor and wound.

chapters.title: Cases No One Wants
chapters.summary: POV Marguerite. His handler, Okafor, offers him off-ledger work: verifying recordings too sensitive for official channels. Marguerite recognizes a voice on tape—a delegate supposedly loyal. The beat: complicity creeping in; he tells himself translation isn't testimony, even as he begins keeping copies.

chapters.title: A Voiceprint in Tallinn
chapters.summary: POV Marguerite. A routine authentication request bounces back from a server in Estonia—and it's keyed to his harvested voiceprint. Someone has been collecting him for years. The beat: vertigo; the discovery that his invisibility was itself manufactured, watched, and catalogued by unseen hands.

chapters.title: What the Server Knew
chapters.summary: POV Marguerite. With hacker contact 'Lark,' he glimpses fragments: the delegation's collapse was scheduled, engineered to justify intervention. His own voice unlocks the archive because he was meant to find it—or be found with it. Beat: paranoia blooming into purpose.

chapters.title: Okafor's Warning
chapters.summary: POV Okafor. The handler warns Marguerite to stop digging, revealing just enough to suggest Okafor is squeezed between masters. A dead courier's name surfaces. Beat: loyalty tested; Okafor's affection for Marguerite curdles into fear for him.

chapters.title: Elena Vasquez Sings
chapters.summary: POV Elena. Introduced in a safehouse outside Riga: a defector analyst whose testimony could expose the engineered collapse—if she reaches the extraction point alive. She suspects she's bait. Beat: fierce, weary intelligence; a woman deciding whom to trust with her life.

chapters.title: The Assignment
chapters.summary: POV Marguerite. Okafor assigns him to escort Elena to the dawn flight—not as interpreter, but as extractor, because his face is unknown and his voice opens doors. Beat: dread and strange exhilaration; invisibility repurposed as a weapon.

chapters.title: First Contact
chapters.summary: POV alternating. Marguerite meets Elena in a rain-soaked transit hub; their first exchange is a test, each probing the other's handlers and motives. She quotes something only the server should contain. Beat: mutual recognition—two professionals fluent in deception meeting someone who might see through them.

chapters.title: The Long Night Begins
chapters.summary: POV Marguerite. They move through Riga's outskirts as checkpoints multiply; the city is being quietly sealed ahead of schedule. Someone leaked the timeline. Beat: the clock tightening; trust built in increments between lies.

chapters.title: Lark Goes Dark
chapters.summary: POV Marguerite. Their hacker contact stops responding mid-message; the last fragment suggests Lark was traced through Marguerite's own access. Guilt lands hard. Beat: the price of survival made literal—his curiosity may have killed an ally.

chapters.title: Bait Theory
chapters.summary: POV Elena. She lays out the trap hypothesis: she was released precisely so someone would extract her, exposing the network. Marguerite realizes he may be the intended catch, not the rescuer. Beat: love against duty takes shape—they must decide whether to keep moving together knowing they might be each other's undoing.

chapters.title: Checkpoint at the River
chapters.summary: POV Marguerite. A bridge crossing goes wrong; Elena talks them past a suspicious officer using Marguerite's coaching, but a tail photographs them. Beat: first bloodless victory, immediately shadowed by the certainty that their faces are now currency.

chapters.title: Okafor's Choice
chapters.summary: POV Okafor. Pressured to confirm Marguerite as compromised, Okafor falsifies a report instead—buying hours, not days. Beat: the handler becomes a co-conspirator; duty bending toward love in its quietest form.

chapters.title: The Safehouse That Wasn't
chapters.summary: POV Elena. Their fallback safehouse is already occupied—by men waiting for them. A near-miss escape through coal cellars leaves Marguerite grazed by a bullet. Beat: the trap confirmed; adrenaline bonding sharpening into something neither will name yet.

chapters.title: Confessions at 3 A.M.
chapters.summary: POV alternating. Hiding in a derelict chapel, they trade true stories—her betrayal of her agency, his decade of erasure. For one hour they are not assets or handlers, just people. Beat: belonging, finally tasted, making everything that follows cost more.

chapters.title: The Flight Moves Up
chapters.summary: POV Marguerite. The extraction window shifts two hours earlier; the airfield route is compromised, forcing a plan through the cargo district. Okafor sends one word: RUN. Beat: desperation with structure—every option bad, one merely survivable.

chapters.title: Cargo District Chase
chapters.summary: POV alternating. A running pursuit through container yards; Elena doubles back to draw tails off Marguerite, refusing to be protected at his expense. Beat: love against duty fully ignited—each trying to spend themselves to save the other.

chapters.title: The Voice That Opens Doors
chapters.summary: POV Marguerite. Cornered at a locked freight gate, Marguerite uses his harvested voiceprint deliberately for the first time—turning the surveillance apparatus into their key. Beat: reclamation; the thing built to own him becomes his instrument.

chapters.title: Dawn Runway
chapters.summary: POV Elena. On the tarmac under searchlights, the plane idles and the net closes; Okafor arrives in person to hold the perimeter with nothing but authority and nerve. Beat: climax pressure—seconds measured in engine noise.

chapters.title: What Marguerite Gives Up
chapters.summary: POV Marguerite. To clear Elena's path, he surrenders himself briefly to the pursuers, trading his identity documents and cooperation for her wheels-up. Beat: the price of survival paid in full—invisibility destroyed so that she can live visible and free.

chapters.title: Aftermath, Tallinn
chapters.summary: POV Elena. Weeks later, the server evidence breaks publicly; the engineered collapse is exposed. Elena, safe, works to locate the man who saved her, following the only thread left: a voiceprint. Beat: grief braided with resolve; love refusing to accept duty's verdict.

chapters.title: When the Asset Sings
chapters.summary: POV Marguerite, then shared. In a small coastal town under a new name, Marguerite answers a knock expecting hunters and finds Elena, having traced him by voice alone. He chooses to stay found. Final beat: resolution—belonging chosen over safety, identity rebuilt not as anonymity but as a self freely given.
